I have farmed these 20 mu in Quzhou County for 25 years. My husband and my son work in construction and factory jobs in the county town, so except for wheat harvest/maize planting in early June and the autumn wheat planting in October, I manage the day-to-day fieldwork myself. We have a well, and I use it because rainfall on the North China Plain never comes when the crops really need it.

This year I will continue the wheat-maize rotation on all 20 mu. In October I will rotary till the fields and sow improved wheat seed from the county supply store. I have learned that these improved varieties stand up better and get sick less than saving my own grain. I spread compound fertilizer as a base before planting, and when the wheat greens up in spring I top-dress with urea. I will irrigate three times from the well: at jointing, at heading, and once during grain filling. Electricity for pumping costs money, but three times is the minimum to get a decent crop here. I will spray twice — once for weeds in early spring, and once later for aphids or rust if they appear, which they usually do.

Immediately after wheat harvest in early June, I will plant hybrid maize with almost no tillage. There is only a narrow window before the soil dries hard, and with my men away at work I cannot afford to spend days preparing the ground. Hybrid seed is costly, but I will not plant anything else — the yield gap is too large to ignore. I apply fertilizer with the planter and side-dress once when the plants are at the big trumpet stage. I will irrigate once or twice over the summer, depending on the rains, especially during silking and grain filling. I spray twice: one early application for weeds, and one for corn borer if the moths show up.

If the weather is normal, I expect about 450 kg of wheat per mu and 550 kg of maize per mu. This plan fits our household labor and brings in enough grain for our own use plus surplus to sell.
